en.h1: Tango, La Boca and the Obelisk: What to See in Buenos Aires, Argentina
en.title: Buenos Aires Travel Guide | What to See, Best Places & Tips
content_excerpts: Embark on a culinary adventure with our food tours in Buenos Aires, where you can indulge in the flavors of Argentina's vibrant capital. These tours are the perfect way to experience one of the world’s most dynamic cities, combining delicious food with rich culture. Plan your trip to include walking tours that explore the stunning landscapes and famous sites around the city, from breathtaking beaches to iconic neighborhoods.

Buenos Aires, the third-largest city in Argentina, is a top destination for tourists, offering much more than just food. The city’s lively culture comes to life with its famous dancing scenes, and there's always a party to join. Our personal travel guides will ensure you don't miss any of the essential activities, from day trips to nearby attractions to immersing yourself in the local nightlife.

Whether you're visiting in March or another time, Buenos Aires is a city that never disappoints. With our services, we'll put together a personalized itinerary that highlights the best of what this incredible city has to offer, making your trip to Argentina truly unforgettable.

For a different experience, spend an entire day at a Gaucho show on an "estancia"—a traditional ranch in the Argentine Pampas (Pampa Humeda) where large cattle are raised. Here, you'll dive into the authentic Gaucho lifestyle, welcomed by hosts with "espadas," mouthwatering barbecue, fine Argentine wine, lively folk music, and traditional dances. Enjoy horseback riding, witness skilled equestrian performances, and take in the excitement of "sortija" and "cuadreras" races.

en.h1: Jesuit Block and colonial architecture: what to see in Cordoba
en.title: Cordoba Travel Guide | What to See, Best Places & Tips
content_excerpts: Córdoba exudes colonial charm and vibrant character. As the educational hub of Argentina, home to seven universities, Córdoba boasts a dynamic atmosphere that many consider unparalleled in the country.

In 2006, Córdoba was honored as the Cultural Capital of the Americas, a testament to its rich colonial heritage and vibrant atmosphere. While it is Argentina's second-largest city after Buenos Aires, Córdoba stands out for its exceptionally well-preserved colonial architecture. Highlights include the stunning 17th-century Manzana Jesuítica (Jesuit Block) with its subterranean Jesuit crypts, Argentina's oldest university, and the historic cabildo (town hall) located on Plaza San Martín. Its unique charm will make you reluctant to leave.

en.h1: Perito Moreno Glacier and Patagonia: what to see in El Calafate
en.title: El Calafate Travel Guide | What to See, Best Places & Tips
content_excerpts: Discover the flavors of Argentina with our food tours in El Calafate, Patagonia, a city renowned for its breathtaking landscapes and unique culture. Plan a trip that includes not only food tours but also a range of activities to immerse yourself in the stunning beauty of Patagonia.

El Calafate, one of Argentina's most visited cities, offers much more than just culinary delights. Experience the stunning landscapes with day trips that highlight the region's natural wonders. Whether you're interested in walking tours around the city or seeking out the perfect spot to enjoy local cuisine, our personal guides will ensure you make the most of your visit.

Its main tourist attraction is the spectacular Perito Moreno Glacier in Los Glaciares National Park. It can be divided into two parts, in the north and south, with El Calafate on Lago Argentino as the gateway. The park is the second largest in Argentina, extending about 170 km along the Chilean border and covering about 759,000 hectares. It was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1987. About 40% of the park is covered by gigantic ice fields, with 47 main glaciers, 13 of which flow east down the park to feed the two great lakes, Lake Viedma, in north and Lago Argentino in the south. There are also about 190 smaller glaciers that are not connected to the ice fields. All together a great show that you have to see.

en.h1: Iguazu Falls and the Devil's Throat: what to see in Puerto Iguazu
en.title: Puerto Iguazu Travel Guide | What to See, Best Places & Tips
content_excerpts: Puerto Iguazú undoubtedly secured its place on the global tourist map thanks to the breathtaking Iguazú Falls. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984, these majestic falls can be admired from both the Argentine and Brazilian sides. While Puerto Iguazú is smaller and more tranquil compared to its Brazilian neighbor, Foz do Iguaçu, it offers equally close access to the stunning waterfalls.

Rising higher than Niagara Falls and stretching twice as wide with 275 cascades arranged in a dramatic horseshoe over nearly two miles of the Iguaçu River, the Iguazú Falls are a striking natural wonder formed by a volcanic eruption that created a massive fissure in the earth. A visit to these falls offers a truly awe-inspiring experience, where the sheer power and thunderous roar of the cascades leave an indelible impression. Alongside Nahuel Huapi National Park in Patagonia, Iguazú Falls ranks as one of Argentina's most popular tourist destinations. Visitors are treated to breathtaking views, with opportunities for guided tours, trekking, and water sports at the base of this majestic site.

en.h1: Train to the Clouds and Seven Colors Mountain: what to see in Salta
en.title: Salta Travel Guide | What to See, Best Places & Tips

Salta stands out for its geographic and climatic heterogeneity, from the desert coldness of the Andes and the Puna to the subtropical heat of the jungle, with cool fertile valleys, mountains and rivers in between.

Salta is the gateway to the Andes of Argentina and it is definitely a city with different cultural traits from the rest of the country with more indigenous people, music and arts that are more synonymous to the Andean region of South America, as commonly found in Bolivia and Peru.

content_excerpts: Placencia resort in Belize in the Caribbean Tours & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Belize  with Ada Tours

Placencia, a stunning emerald peninsula in southern Belize, boasts 16 miles of pristine sandy beaches. To the east lies the sparkling Caribbean Sea, while the serene Placencia Lagoon to the west is framed by the majestic mountains of the mainland. The peninsula is naturally divided into two sections: the area south of the airstrip and the area north of it. Exploring Placencia is a breeze with a beach cruiser bike, allowing you to easily navigate this picturesque locale. The southern part of Placencia is the bustling hub, home to a vibrant mix of coffee shops, bistros, internet cafes, the harbor, guesthouses, and essential services like taxi and bus stations, banks, and local eateries.

The northern section of Placencia, which encompasses the Garifuna village of Seine Bight, is more sparsely populated and features several upscale resorts. Situated farther from the reef, this area experiences genuine, albeit modest, surf. The waters here are crystal clear, with gentle trade winds providing a refreshing breeze. Few experiences are as tranquil as watching a Belizean sunset from a secluded beach on the Placencia Peninsula, offering a serene and soul-soothing escape.

en.title: Punta Gorda Tours & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Belize  with Ada Tours
content_excerpts: Nestled on the western shores of the Caribbean Sea, Punta Gorda Town graces the southern expanse of Belize, where it serves as the gateway to the Gulf of Honduras. This coastal town is more than just a picturesque locale; it stands as the administrative heart of the Toledo District, a region rich in cultural heritage and natural beauty.

Punta Gorda is your portal to the wonders of the Toledo District, where adventure meets history at every turn. Whether you're casting a line in the turquoise waters offshore, navigating serene rivers, exploring hidden caves, or marveling at the vibrant birdlife, Punta Gorda offers an unparalleled introduction to Belize’s treasures. The district's rich tapestry of Maya archaeological sites and natural wonders ensures that every traveler finds something extraordinary to discover.

The city in Amatique Bay on the Caribbean coast is ideal for both passive and active recreation. A number of sandy beaches stretch along the city coastline. There is a market on the main street of Punta Gorda, where you can feel not only the local flavor, but also the whole of Belize, buy handmade products from different parts of the country.

To top it all off, Toledo is a district not only filled with natural beauty in abundance but also home to some of the nicest people. Here Maya, Garifuna and East Indian Belizeans live harmoniously while maintaining their individual cultures.

Visitors are also drawn to the town's charming, frontier-style wooden shops lining its narrow streets, where they can indulge in shopping and savor delightful local cuisine.

Embark on an unforgettable trip to Lake Titicaca, the highest navigable lake in the world, with one of our expertly crafted Bolivia tours. Whether you're seeking a guided tour to Lake Titicaca or planning to explore on your own, our travel packages are designed to showcase the best of this stunning region.

Choose a tour to Lake Titicaca that fits your interests, from exploring the floating islands of the Uros people to discovering the rich cultural heritage of the region. Our Bolivia travel packages offer a seamless experience, ensuring that your journey is both enriching and hassle-free.

Whether you're embarking on a short trip or an extended adventure, our Bolivia tours provide a perfect blend of cultural immersion and natural beauty. Let us help you craft the ideal package for your travels, making your trip to Lake Titicaca a highlight of your South American adventure.

The principal town on the shores of Lake Titicaca is Copacabana, a vibrant hub from which boats depart for the mystical Isla del Sol. This town is home to the impressive 16th-century Basilica of Our Lady of Copacabana, dedicated to Bolivia's patron saint. Renowned across the country, Copacabana is celebrated for its rich cultural heritage, religious festivities, and traditional festivals that draw visitors year-round. Nestled between Mount Calvario and Mount Niño Calvario, this charming town is home to about 6,000 residents and offers a unique blend of spiritual significance and local tradition.

The name "Copacabana" is commonly believed to come from the Aymara phrase kota kahuana, which means "view of the lake." However, social scientist Mario Montaño Aragón uncovered an intriguing alternative in the "Archives of Indias" in Seville, Spain. He discovered that "Kotakawana" refers to an ancient Andean fertility deity, akin to the Greek goddess Aphrodite or the Roman Venus. This androgynous god is said to reside in Lake Titicaca, accompanied by mythical beings known as "Umantuus," akin to mermaids in Western lore, depicted in colonial sculptures.

Remarkably, the current Basilica of Our Lady of Copacabana stands on the site of the ancient Temple of Kotakawana, a sacred place long before the Spanish arrival. Today, small fertility temples dedicated to Kotakawana can still be found along the shores of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia and Peru, underscoring the area’s profound spiritual significance that predates colonial history.

en.h1: La Paz Tours
en.title: La Paz, the capital of Bolivia Tours  & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Bolivia  with Ada Tours
content_excerpts: La Paz, the capital of Bolivia Tours  & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Bolivia  with Ada Tours

La Paz, aptly called the city that touches the sky, truly lives up to its name. Perched at an impressive altitude of 3,660 meters (12,008 feet), it is the highest capital city in the world. Nestled within a natural bowl surrounded by the high-altitude plains, the city’s sprawling neighborhoods climb the surrounding hills, reaching elevations between 3,000 and 4,100 meters. Dominating the skyline is the majestic, snow-capped Illimani, a triple-peaked sentinel that watches over the city. Serving as both the administrative and departmental capital of Bolivia, La Paz boasted a population of 789,585 according to the 2001 census. When combined with the neighboring cities of El Alto and Viacha, it forms Bolivia's most populous urban area, with over 1.6 million residents.

La Paz stands as Bolivia’s cultural heart, brimming with vibrant marketplaces that are woven into the city's fabric, ensuring you encounter them wherever you wander. The city also boasts a rich tapestry of museums and historical landmarks. Key sites include the Cathedral of San Francisco, where the saint's remains are interred; the Metropolitan Cathedral, which houses the remains of Sucre; and the Quemado Palace, the seat of the executive branch.

You can also visit the Congress building, which occasionally opens its doors to the public, and stroll along Jaen Street, a preserved relic from the Spanish era, home to ten intriguing museums. Other notable attractions are the Valle de la Luna (Valley of the Moon) and the Muela del Diablo (Devil's Tooth), a striking geological formation ideal for hiking. Don’t miss the Cine-Teatro Municipal, a 19th-century gem, the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés, the largest state university in Bolivia, and the General Cemetery, the resting place of many Bolivian presidents. Explore the historic house of Simon Bolivar and take in the unique landscapes and cultural landmarks that make La Paz a city like no other.

The city is ideally situated close to a wealth of natural wonders and ancient ruins. Many visitors opt for day trips to the Tiahuanacu ruins, which, predating Machu Picchu by thousands of years, hold equal historical significance. The allure of Tiahuanacu is so strong that Chilean and Peruvian itineraries often feature this site, despite it being located in Bolivia. Another popular excursion is to Lake Titicaca and the lakeside town of Copacabana, renowned for its cathedral, which houses the revered Virgen de Copacabana, a significant deity of the lake.

Nestled between Mount Calvario and Mount Niño Calvario, this charming town is home to about 6,000 residents and offers a unique blend of spiritual significance and local tradition.

The name "Copacabana" is commonly believed to come from the Aymara phrase kota kahuana, which means "view of the lake." However, social scientist Mario Montaño Aragón uncovered an intriguing alternative in the "Archives of Indias" in Seville, Spain. He discovered that "Kotakawana" refers to an ancient Andean fertility deity, akin to the Greek goddess Aphrodite or the Roman Venus. This androgynous god is said to reside in Lake Titicaca, accompanied by mythical beings known as "Umantuus," akin to mermaids in Western lore, depicted in colonial sculptures.

Remarkably, the current Basilica of Our Lady of Copacabana stands on the site of the ancient Temple of Kotakawana, a sacred place long before the Spanish arrival. Today, small fertility temples dedicated to Kotakawana can still be found along the shores of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia and Peru, underscoring the area’s profound spiritual significance that predates colonial history.

en.h1: Oruro Tours
en.title: Oruro, Bolivia   Tours & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Bolivia with Ada Tours
content_excerpts: Oruro, Bolivia   Tours & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Bolivia with Ada Tours

Oruro, a Bolivian city with a population exceeding 215,660 as of 2001, sits approximately midway between La Paz and Sucre at an elevation of about 3,710 meters above sea level. As the capital of the Oruro department, the city has a rich history, originally established in 1606 as a silver mining hub in the Urus region. Initially named Real Villa de Don Felipe de Austria in honor of Spanish monarch Philip III, Oruro eventually fell into decline as its silver resources were depleted.

Oruro’s tranquil daily life transforms dramatically during its renowned carnival, one of South America's most authentic folklore celebrations. This vibrant festival draws tourists from across the globe. Additionally, Oruro boasts a symphony orchestra and several historic churches dating back to the 18th and 19th centuries. It also serves as the headquarters for the Roman Catholic Diocese of Oruro, further enriching its cultural and religious significance.

Oruro was reestablished in the late nineteenth century, as a tin mining center. For a time, the La Salvadora tin mine was the most important source of tin in the world. Gradually, this resource was also exhausted, and Oruro again went into a decline. The city does manage, however, to attract tourists to its carnival, the Carnaval de Oruro, considered one of the great folkloric events in South America for its masked "devil dances". Oruro was named after the native tribe "Uru-Uru". The city is the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Oruro. The Oruro Symphony Orchestra is based in Oruro.

en.h1: Potosí Tours
en.title: Potosí, Bolivia Tours & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Potosi  with Ada Tours
content_excerpts: Potosí, Bolivia Tours & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Potosi  with Ada Tours

Potosí, the capital of Bolivia's Potosí department, is often celebrated as the highest city in the world, perched at an altitude of approximately 4,090 meters. The city is situated at the foot of Cerro de Potosí, colloquially known as Cerro Rico or "rich mountain," which has historically overshadowed the city with its legendary silver deposits. The peak of Cerro de Potosí reaches an impressive 4,824 meters (15,827 feet) above sea level, adding to the city's dramatic and storied landscape.

Despite their striking beauty, the churches of Potosí were built through the harsh labor of enslaved workers. These grand edifices starkly juxtapose the professed Christian values of the Spanish mine owners who financed them with the grim realities of the mining conditions they enforced. It was said that while divine authority was proclaimed in Potosí’s 34 churches, the Devil reveled in the city’s six thousand mines, highlighting the profound contradiction between faith and exploitation.

Potosí’s churches, adorned with intricately carved porticos and lavishly gilded interiors, stand as prime examples of the mestizo-Baroque style, blending European Christian motifs with indigenous Andean symbols. These churches were not only a testament to religious devotion but also an expression of gratitude for the immense wealth generated by the city. Unusually, Potosí’s churches face south toward the imposing Cerro Rico, rather than the typical westward orientation of Catholic churches. This orientation reflects both the city's spiritual significance and its role in the conversion of the indigenous population. With hundreds of thousands of indigenous workers from various ethnic groups laboring under the mita system, Potosí became an ideal setting for religious indoctrination. In addition to numerous churches and convents built for Spanish use, the Spaniards constructed fourteen parish churches specifically for the indigenous mitayos, underscoring their efforts to integrate and convert the local populace.

en.h1: Santa Cruz Tours in Bolivia
en.title: Santa Cruz, Bolivia Tours & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Bolivia  with Ada Tours
content_excerpts: Santa Cruz, Bolivia Tours & Vacation packages | Guided trips to Bolivia  with Ada Tours

Santa Cruz de la Sierra, the capital of the Department of Santa Cruz, is situated in the eastern region of Bolivia. As a burgeoning, vibrant metropolis, Santa Cruz stands out for its modernity and commercial energy. Over the past decade, this thriving city has expanded rapidly, now boasting a population exceeding 1.5 million and earning its status as the nation's economic hub. The city's layout features concentric circles, with the historic core, known as Casco Viejo, nestled within the innermost ring.

Santa Cruz offers a vibrant nightlife scene, with a plethora of options for evening entertainment. The city boasts an array of clubs, bars, discos, and pubs, as well as a variety of dining experiences ranging from grills and restaurants to pastry shops and ice cream parlors. Live music venues are also plentiful. The area surrounding the main square, "24 de Septiembre," features numerous bar and restaurant establishments, making it a lively hub for socializing and enjoying the local flavor.

In the early 20th century, Santa Cruz emerged as a significant player in Bolivia's history, largely influenced by two key conflicts: the war with Brazil at the turn of the century and the Chaco War with Paraguay in the 1930s. During this period, Santa Cruz was somewhat cut off from the rest of the nation, with its first major road link to Cochabamba not established until the 1950s. The subsequent connection via rail to Brazil further spurred the city's economic and demographic expansion, transforming it into a pivotal center of growth.

en.h1: Sucre, the white city of Bolivia
en.title: Excursions and tours to Sucre, Bolivia
content_excerpts: Proud, genteel Sucre is Bolivia’s most beautiful city and the symbolic heart of the nation. It was here that independence was proclaimed and while La Paz is now the seat of government and treasury, Sucre is recognized in the constitution as the nation’s capital.

Set in a valley surrounded by low mountains, Sucre enjoys a mild and comfortable climate. It’s still a center of learning and both the city and its university enjoy reputations as focal points of progressive thought within the country.
May 25th Square (Plaza 25 de Mayo) is the most visited place. There is a cathedral and a town hall, there is a monument to Jose Antonio Sucre, the second president of independent Bolivia.

A glorious ensemble of whitewashed buildings sheltering pretty patios, it’s a spruce place that preserves a wealth of colonial architecture. Sensibly, there are strict controls on development, which have ensured Sucre remains a real showpiece of Bolivia. It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991.

en.h1: Salar de Uyuni
en.title: Excursions and Tours to Uyuni, Salt Flats Bolivia
content_excerpts: If a Bolivian Salt Flats tour isn’t on your travel bucket list, add it now.  The Salt Flats themselves are the definite highlight of the tour, but they only constitute one of the four days of the trip.  This is actually a tour of southwestern Bolivia, and never in my life have I felt more like an astronaut.

Other-worldly landscapes await you on this indescribable jeep trip through scenes out of a fantasy land.  Red and green colored lagoons, pink flamingos and other unique wildlife, geysers, volcanoes, and geothermal wonders, painted mountains, bizarre rock formations, and the feeling of being on the moon are just a sampling of the highlights of the other three days. Then there’s the Salt Flats themselves.  The highest and largest in the world, the Salt Flats are a wonder like no other. Bright white stretching as far as the eye can see, contrasting with the deep blue skies, offers a scene that simply doesn’t look, seem, or feel real.  A magical place that has people of every age acting like children, a trip to the Salar de Uyuni is a memorable one.
Salar de Uyuni is the most photographed site in Bolivia and is what draws many people to the country.

en.h1: Oscar Niemeyer's Architecture and Pampulla Park: What to See in Belo Horizonte
en.title: Belo Horizonte, Brazil: Attractions and Travel Guide to the Garden City
content_excerpts: Known to the locals as Beagá (pronounced 'bay-ah-gah', Portuguese for BH), Belo Horizonte was named for its beautiful view of nearby mountains. Urban sprawl makes it harder to appreciate the natural setting nowadays, but Brazil’s third-largest city still has considerable charm.

A distinctive feature of Belo Horizonte is a large number of green areas with an unusual design. There are about 2 million different trees growing here. This is a real garden city, where thousands of tourists come every year. Pampulla Ecological Park is one of those interesting objects that cannot be missed. It is decorated with the works of the famous Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer.

Walk down the buzzing cosmopolitan streets of the Savassi neighborhood on a Saturday evening, eat at one of the fine restaurants in Lourdes, stroll through the densely packed stalls at Mercado Central, attend a weekend street fair or a concert at the Palácio das Artes, or visit the Inhotim art museum west of the city, and you’ll see that Belo Horizonte has countless dimensions. Add to all this the friendly, welcoming nature of Beagá’s people and you’ve got a winning combination. Stick around a few days – you might grow fond of the place.

en.h1: Blue Lake Cave and Snorkeling: What to See in Bonito, Brazil
en.title: Bonito, Brazil: Attractions and Travel Guide to Ecotourism Paradise
content_excerpts: In Portuguese, the word Bonito means beautiful, too modest to describe the totality of the beauty of this exotic area.
The natural beauties in Bonito include caverns with deep azure lakes inside, incredibly clear rivers that work as natural aquariums, hundreds of waterfalls and much more.
Bonito is a unique place where ancient trees, diverse fauna and the purest transparent rivers form a single complex, and all this makes Bonito an ideal ecotourism destination.

Bonito is a paradise in the south of the Pantanal.  The Blue Lake Cave is the most famous destination in the outside of Bonito. Stalactites and stalagmites of various shapes grow towards each other. The lake occupies a significant part of the cave, and although from a scientific point of view it is possible to explain its amazing color due to a certain angle of sunlight, yet the effect of a surprisingly blue color is amazing. The Blue Lake Cave is one of the largest and oldest flooded caves in the world. In 1992, an expedition of Brazilian paleontologists discovered the fossilized remains of mammals buried at the bottom of the cave - the prehistoric skeletons of a giant sloth and a saber-toothed tiger.

en.h1: Niemeyer's Architecture: What to See in Brasilia, a UNESCO World Heritage City
en.title: Brasilia: Attractions and Travel Guide to the UNESCO World Heritage City
content_excerpts: Brazil's capital, Brasília, is truly one-of-a-kind. Designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it stands as a prime illustration of 20th-century modernism in both architecture and urban planning. Brasília is more than just a city with a master plan; it represents a meticulously designed capital from the ground up.

Inaugurated on April 22, 1960, Brasília, Brazil's capital, was established in the heart of the country. Merely five years prior, the region was a barren expanse, devoid of inhabitants and characterized by limited water resources, sparse wildlife, and minimal vegetation.
Book your tour in the capital of Brazil, the most colorful country of Latin America!

Oscar Niemeyer's major project in Brasília is the Cathedral of Brasília, known as the Cathedral Metropolitana de Nossa Senhora Aparecida, which is one of the most famous monuments of the 20th century and a masterpiece of Niemeyer. Brasília is the cultural heart of the country, featuring the National Theater, the Museum of Brazil, and the Institute of History. The city's zoo houses exotic animals from the Amazon rainforest, which can only be seen there. Brasília also offers a range of entertainment options. The park adjacent to the television tower covers a vast natural reserve and includes facilities for relaxation: monorail tracks, playgrounds, bike paths, a fishing lake, and a pool with artificial waves.
